It builds on the observation that rasterizing triangles from a single direction leaves gaps, and that rotating triangles to their dominant axis is a computationally cheaper alternative to full 3D rotation matrices [S1, S2, unofficial].

The claim consists of two main parts: 1) Rasterizing triangles from a single direction leaves gaps, and 2) Rotating triangles to their dominant axis is a computationally cheaper alternative to full 3D rotation matrices. Source [S1] explicitly states that rasterizing from a single direction 'can leave large gaps in the 3D texture if surfaces are not facing the camera' and describes the 'Dominant Axis Selection' technique where triangles are rotated (via coordinate permutation, which is a specific type of orthogonal rotation) to expose the surface. Source [S2] explicitly contrasts this method with 'fully rotating it on 3d so that it becomes flat on the same plane,' stating that the latter is a 'much more expensive operation' with a 'non-negligible impact in your performance,' whereas the dominant axis method is 'quick dirty and simple.' Thus, the evidence supports both the problem (gaps) and the solution's efficiency relative to full 3D rotation.
